items.album: Mikkel Rev / Evocation (ASIPV057)
items.body:
Enter the Magnetic Heliosphere. 

 Mikkel Rev returns to A Strangely Isolated Place with Evocation , his third full-length album shaped deep within the forests of Norway. 

 Since Mikkel’s debut, The Art of Levitation first arrived in 2023, Mikkel has been quietly building his own corner of the ASIP catalogue. Last year's Journey Beyond expanded that vision further, revealing an artist increasingly comfortable balancing the emotional pull of early trance with a more reflective, ambient-leaning approach. While his work elsewhere naturally gravitates towards the dance floor through his own collective, Ute Recordings and other club-focused outlets, his ASIP releases have always evolved differently. Beginning with a larger body of material that’s gradually shaped together, each album seeks to find a narrative without a dancefloor in place; one that moves naturally between momentum and stillness, carrying something of the spirit found in those early-'90s records that drifted effortlessly between peak-time energy and the quiet hours in room two. 

 astrangelyisolatedplace · Mikkel Rev / Evocation (ASIPV057) [Previews] 

 Long-form compositions like "Step Inside" and "MRI" favor gradual development over immediate impact, while "Dream Sand" introduces shimmering rhythms that subtly shift the album's momentum and pace. The piano-led "The Infinite" offers a definitive nod to the enduring emotional pull of classic trance before "Sanitorium" closes the record with one of Mikkel's most restrained and affecting pieces to date.

 Evocation continues Mikkel Rev's remarkable run on ASIP, extending a catalog where echoes of trance's formative years find new expression through the communal energy and natural surroundings of the Nordic forest gatherings that have become an integral part of his world.

 Ventral Is Golden returns on artwork duties, with Lupo handling the mastering and cut. Released on August 28th as a gatefold double LP on dusty purple smoke and digital.

items.body: My daughter and I walked up Seventh Avenue on a balmy, post-thunderstorm July night to one of the most well-known, and most sacred, of all jazz venues on the planet, the storied Village Vanguard, to catch the opening night of a week-long residence by the trio Paradoxical Frog. Readers of the Free Jazz Blog might care to know this was a historical occasion and one that involved the reuniting of three musicians often discussed here at the FJC: pianist Kris Davis, saxophonist Ingrid Laubrock, and drummer Tyshawn Sorey. Behind the famous red doors that evening would perform an avant-garde trio that had not played together in over a decade. And the band’s unconventional leanings are perhaps less alien to the Vanguard than one might first guess. Davis and Sorey have performed at the Vanguard countless times, and Laubrock’s appearance is as rare and welcome as the recent celebrated stint of the James Brandon Lewis Quartet in the West Village club. This is to say nothing of the audience in the house that night: I spotted Sylvie Courvoisier a few seats behind me, and encountered William Parker outside the doors after the first set had concluded. Davis actually opened the show fact-checking the record. “I was corrected on social media,” she said. “It has not been fifteen years since the three of us played together; it has been eleven.” In any case, for listeners to either of the group’s two Cleanfeed recordings, 2010’s Paradoxical Frog , and 2012’s Union , it had been a long wait to hear these three masters perform in this distinct context. The opening night’s set consisted of four long compositions, all of which have appeared on record at some point. The first performance, a combination of Laubrock’s “Masterisk” and Davis’s “Union” spanned over twenty-nine minutes. Seeing the work live allowed me to confirm just how through-composed these Paradoxical Frog pieces are. Note the extensive paper scores in Davis’s and Sorey’s hands and the extensions on Laubrock’s music stand: a necessary tool to display the lengthy writings of each work without requiring the saxophonist to flip pages of these surprising compositions that challenge functional harmony and defy circular rhythm. The third work was “Whistlings” from 2020’s Blood Moon , the Intakt Records duo of Davis and Laubrock. The live performance, over twice the length of the original recording, featured Laubrock on soprano saxophone and Tyshawn Sorey on a sonic array of material, at times the room so quiet that Sorey’s percussion would consist of simply waving his brushes in the air, an effect that hauntingly filled the room with audible whisperings. The set concluded with Sorey’s “Slow Burn,” clocking in at over sixteen minutes and featuring the mysterious repetition of single notes on Davis’s piano keys. It was moving to see these three unite again, and I am certain I do not speak alone in voicing my hopes for more work in the future, maybe even a Live at the Village Vanguard recording to place among some of the mythical voices who have passed through that hallowed underground room. items.body:
BTS have announced that they will not submit their music for consideration at the 69th Grammy Awards, set to take place in February 2027.

The group shared the news via Instagram Stories across all seven members' accounts on 29 July, revealing that they had decided against entering this year's awards cycle.

"We have decided not to submit to the Grammys this year. We hope music can be heard and embraced for what it is, beyond region or language. Thank you to ARMY and everyone who continues to support us," the group wrote.

The decision comes just weeks after the Recording Academy introduced Best Asian Pop Music Performance, a new category that will debut at the 2027 Grammys. Created to recognise excellence in Asian pop music, the award covers works in one or more Asian languages, including K-pop, J-pop, and C-pop.

The addition of the category has sparked widespread discussion across the music industry. While some have welcomed it as long-overdue recognition of Asian pop's global influence, others have questioned whether it creates a separate lane for Asian artists rather than recognising them alongside other acts in the Grammys' General Field categories.

Although BTS did not explain the reason behind their decision beyond their statement, the timing has led many fans and industry observers to connect it to the newly introduced category.

The announcement is particularly notable given the group's long-standing history with the Recording Academy. Over the years, BTS have openly spoken about winning a Grammy as one of their career ambitions. They previously earned Grammy nominations for 'Dynamite', 'Butter', and 'My Universe', but have yet to take home a trophy.

Earlier this year, the septet made a record-breaking return with ARIRANG, their first full-length studio album in six years. The album debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, while lead single 'SWIM' topped the Billboard Hot 100, further cementing the group's global impact.

Whether or not BTS return to Grammy consideration in future years remains to be seen, but their latest decision has reignited conversations about how global music—and particularly Asian artists—are recognised on one of music's biggest stages.

ZELO is keeping the summer vibes alive with the release of his latest single via VLACKSQUAD, 'ELA', marking the next step in the South Korean artist's evolving musical journey.

Following the release of 'Cola Comigo', the former B.A.P member continues to lean into Latin-pop influences, blending breezy rhythms with smooth R&B sensibilities and polished global pop production. The result is a track built for late-night drives, festival singalongs, and sun-soaked playlists.

Anchored by a dreamy electric guitar and tropical-inspired production, 'ELA' pairs rhythmic percussion with an infectious melodic hook. ZELO's vocals effortlessly glide between melodic passages and rhythmic delivery, highlighting the versatility he has continued to develop as a solo artist.

While 'Cola Comigo' introduced his Latin-pop direction, 'ELA' expands on that foundation by weaving together Latin-inspired grooves, contemporary R&B, and ZELO's signature performance style. Rather than chasing trends, the single feels like a natural progression of his evolving sound.

'ELA' also taps into the nostalgia of 2010s global pop, recalling memories of festival nights, open-air parties, and unforgettable summer moments while giving that familiar feeling a fresh, modern update.

items.body:
For Réjizz, the future is no longer something waiting around the corner. On his five-track EP The Era, the Bangkok-born rapper, singer, and producer steps fully into the world he first imagined on its predecessor, The New Era. The project captures who he is now—more visible, more assured, and increasingly aware of the pressures that arrive alongside success.

Moving through jazz-infused hip-hop, darker cinematic production, and dance-driven rhythms, The Era places Réjizz’s Thai-Funk sound in several distinct emotional worlds. Across tracks such as 'I've Been Around', 'JRIZ', 'Uncomfortable Situations', 'Long Disco Relationship', and 'In My Position', he reflects on life away from home, modern dating, industry artificiality, long-distance love, and learning to trust his own direction.

In this interview with Bandwagon, Réjizz opens up about creating his most vulnerable project yet, choosing clarity over old vices, and the artistic freedom he hopes to reach in the next phase of his journey.

The Era follows The New Era, which represented the future you were working towards. When did you realise that future had become your present?

Since I started The New Era, I wanted to touch on different styles of music. It was always part of the long-term plan to introduce the audience to a new sound I was working on, and then I cemented the idea with The Era. Now that the EP has been released, it feels like the future has become the present.

You have described The Era as your most vulnerable and “realest” project yet. What were you ready to reveal here that you could not have expressed on your earlier releases?

I was stuck in a situation where my flow state and creativity were suppressed for a long time, and my quality of life suffered because of it. This EP gave me a space to finally express those feelings.

When I was younger, I usually dealt with this by giving in to my vices. This time, I decided to go straight-edge, which gave me clarity and made my writing more vivid than ever before. I wasn’t rushing to write. I carefully chose each word and used different rhyming techniques to express my truest feelings.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Marshall Records (@marshallrecords)

Each track occupies a different sonic and emotional world. What is the thread that connects all five songs and makes them part of the same era?

I’ve always touched on different sounds and universes throughout my projects, but the connecting part is who I am in that project. Réjizz is the connecting thread.

I’m no longer an underground artist trying to prove myself. It’s cool to win an award and be the first Thai artist to sign to Marshall Records, but success comes with new problems, and this project addresses that.

One thing that has been consistent throughout my projects is love. I always find a track or a verse to address that.

On 'I've Been Around', you explore the tension between pursuing the life you worked for and missing home. Has success changed what “home” means to you?

When I’m away, calling my mom or my lady gives me a sense of home for a little while. But it will always feel good to actually be back home.

Last year, I moved back to my childhood home, and that house really feels like home. So “home” to me still means going back and seeing my mom.

'JRIZ' is the EP’s only Thai-language track. Why did this story about modern dating feel most natural to tell in Thai?

A lot of Thai songs are about love anyway. I chose this track to be the most easy-listening one for a mass audience, so I wrote a love song with a slight twist.

'JRIZ' moves between male and female perspectives. How did you write from both sides while keeping each voice honest and nuanced?

At my age, my single friends are moving through the dating world fast. They rant about it to me all the time, so I wanted to use that as the premise of the song and write a verse from both the guy’s and the girl’s perspectives.

Each voice is honest because they are actual lines from friends around me.

'Uncomfortable Situations' transforms the guests at an industry party into aliens and monsters. Was that imagery inspired by a specific experience, or by feelings that built up over time?

The imagery was inspired by a real-life event where a lot of wealthy individuals came to this party to “network”, and a lot of talents were looking to be hired. Everyone connects on a surface level early in the night, but after a few drinks, their true colours start to show.

They say, “You can be famous if you just…” and by the time they finish their thought, it’s like they want you to change your whole identity, like you’re going to lose your soul. I believe a lot of talents change themselves to become famous.

So my analogy for these encounters is aliens and monsters that try to make you become one of them. I still encounter these situations to this day. Every time it happens, this song plays in my head.

In 'Long Disco Relationship', you compare long-distance love to two people trying to stay in step as the music shifts. In real life, what does it take to keep that connection alive?

Communication is the most important thing because it is the only thing you can do when you’re far away. Like on the dance floor, you must stick to the same rhythm to remain connected to each other.

'In My Position' addresses the different voices trying to influence your direction. How have you learned to distinguish meaningful advice from distraction?

Who the advice comes from is always crucial. If they share the same values as me and they’ve accomplished what I strive for, it makes the advice much more credible.

The ones who are a distraction are the ones who don’t align with my values. Usually, they’re trying to steer me into something I’m not.

At the end of the day, my instinct and gut feeling always tell me which one to trust. It’s like my Spidey-sense.

The Era documents who you are in the present. After completing it, what part of yourself are you most curious to explore next?

I am looking forward to the day when I reach my prime—when my working system is stable, I trust the people who work with me, and I have consistent tours. I want enough to make a living, but not so many that they drain my soul. I’ll constantly be in a flow state.

That’s when I’ll be carefree, and my music will be free to become whatever it wants.

I might want to make a trashy trap song one day, then an eloquent jazz-infused Mo Lam song the next. I’ll master English and Thai, seamlessly mixing them in my music. The ideas are unlimited.

That day is when I’ll truly take ownership of my own craft. I’ll probably name it Réjizz Mania or DOIN’ MY THANG. I don’t know—that stage is still to be explored.

items.body:
Tomorrowland Belgium 2026 has officially come to a close after two weekends at De Schorre in Boom, welcoming 400,000 festivalgoers from more than 200 countries while reaching a record-breaking 233 million livestream views across YouTube, TikTok, Facebook, and Instagram.

Held 17–19 July and 24–26 July, this year's edition revolved around Consciencia, a new festival theme exploring six universal emotions — Wonder, Love, Anger, Joy, Desire, and Sadness. Rather than assigning stages solely by genre, Tomorrowland built each of its 16 stages around an emotional identity, with stage design, production, and programming reflecting one of the six themes.

The concept also came to life on the festival's largest Mainstage to date. Standing over 43 metres tall and 140 metres wide, the structure featured towering waterfalls, fountains, lasers, and six giant sculptures representing the emotions at the heart of Consciencia. The ambitious production marked a major return for Tomorrowland following last year's Mainstage fire, which forced organisers to rethink the festival's centrepiece shortly before opening.

Away from the Mainstage, more than 500 artists performed across the festival grounds. Among the standout moments was Calvin Harris' long-awaited Tomorrowland Belgium debut, closing the Mainstage on both Saturdays with a career-spanning set. During Weekend 1, John Newman joined Harris onstage for a live performance of 'Blame', while techno star Charlotte de Witte surprised fans with an unannounced Mainstage appearance after weeks of speculation.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Calvin Harris (@calvinharris)

The festival also had to adapt to unusually dry weather conditions. Belgian authorities imposed restrictions on fireworks and pyrotechnics during the opening weekend because of elevated wildfire risks. While limited close-range effects returned for Weekend 2, Tomorrowland replaced many of its signature fireworks with large-scale LED visuals across the Mainstage screens.

Beyond the music, organisers also teased what's next for the festival brand. A banner displayed near Dreamville hinted at a possible Tomorrowland expansion to Las Vegas in 2027 alongside events in France, Belgium, Brazil, Ibiza, and Thailand, though organisers have yet to officially reveal further details.

Not every headline was celebratory. During the opening weekend, two original paintings commissioned for the Consciencia theme were stolen from the Tomorrowland Restaurant. One artwork, Love, was later recovered and returned before Weekend 2, while Desire remains missing.

For fans watching from around the world, Tomorrowland's digital presence continued to grow. The festival's livestream attracted 233 million views—surpassing last year's 193 million and setting a new record for the event. The figures underline how Tomorrowland has evolved beyond an on-site festival into one of electronic music's largest global broadcast experiences.

The festival also drew a number of familiar faces from Singapore, with radio personality Sonia Chew, content creators Saffron Sharpe and Edo Lio among those spotted at Tomorrowland Belgium 2026.

The trio shared glimpses of their experience on social media, including a meet-up with headlining Dutch DJ Martin Garrix. Check out their posts below for a closer look at their Tomorrowland adventure.

items.body:
Singapore's choral community is set to come together once again as the Voices of Singapore (VOS) Festival returns for its 11th edition, taking place 5–9 September across four venues in the city. The annual event remains Singapore's largest non-competitive choral festival, bringing together singers of all ages for five days of performances, workshops, masterclasses, and community-led musical experiences.

This year's edition will span CHIJMES Hall, Capitol Singapore Outdoor Plaza, VOS Capitol Studios, and, for the first time, the VOS Choral Hub at Enabling Village. The new venue expands the festival's inclusive programming, reflecting the organisation's ongoing efforts to make choral music more accessible to communities across Singapore.

Across the five-day festival, audiences can expect close to 50 programmes, including gala concerts, school choir performances, recitals, outdoor showcases, choir exchanges, workshops, and masterclasses. Rather than focusing on competition, the festival continues to champion collaboration and learning, creating opportunities for choirs to perform, connect, and grow together.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Voices of Singapore (@voicesofsingapore)

Leading this year's artistic programme are internationally acclaimed guest conductors Dr. Jeffery Redding (USA), Mak Chi Hoe (Malaysia), and Lieu Ryland-Jones (Estonia). They will conduct four specially formed Festival Choruses — Children's, Youth, Community, and Virtuosi — while also leading more than 10 masterclasses for Singapore school choirs and five public workshops for music educators and conductors.

Festival highlights also include four gala performances at CHIJMES Hall featuring VOS Choirs, the Filipino Voice Symphony, and the Festival Choruses, alongside six concerts showcasing school choirs from across Singapore. items.body:
There's a scene near the end of  Uncut Gems  where the hapless protagonist Howard Ratner, locked behind the security glass of his own shop, watches a parlay come in leg by leg. As each result lands, the magnitude of the one that follows swells, a runaway train of buzz and anxious sweats. Watching Short Span for the past 18 months has felt a lot like standing behind that glass. (Without giving away spoilers, don't worry, that's where the Ratner comparisons end.)

The Sheffield label, run by Matthew Kent—formerly of 2010s-defining mix series  Blowing Up The Workshop —has yet to lose a bet. From Yu Su's  Foundry  to  K Wata 's  Give U Space , each record raises what's staked on the next.  Uuuuuuuu  from Aarhus producer Picture, AKA Natal Zaks is the latest leg to come in—and it's a delight.
 
On the surface, it might seem like an unlikely match. To this day, Zaks is perhaps better known as  Central , who released slinky, midtempo house music as part of Regelbau (he also gave Erika de Casier her  first credit  back in 2017). Short Span, meanwhile, started out a dub techno label two years ago with notable, genre-bending early releases from Sa Pa and Mammo teeing up a widening of the roster in 2026 with the likes of Mr YT and Bot1500. You might consider the label's releases as having little in common musically—instead, the throughline is a disposition rather than a sound. Yu Su  described  Kent as having "all this in-betweenness going on," never settling into one style; Kent has put it similarly himself,  musing  that the label is "for a certain kind of identity that crosses boundaries."

Zaks, then, makes a perfect fit. There's always been something unresolved about his sound, and the traces are audible if you dig: take " Lost Touch ," from 2022's  Up And Down , a twitchy dub techno number built around a wavering synth and a sense of space you'll recognise from the Picture records. 

 Uuuuuuuu  is Zaks' second Short Span record this year, following February's  Eeeeeeee , and harder than the first. "Peeeeeee" (no relation to it's bodily namesake, seemingly) is a claustrophobic techno number with a swinging bassline and an undercurrent of unease like a wonkier Chain Reaction cut. It's reminiscent of being inside a printing factory: the looping synth line is the chug of the machinery, the filter sweep and textures like flying debris, ramping up in the closing minutes, twisting the dial even further on a sense of anxiety. Similarly, "Wooooooo" conjures up the darkest corners of the club. Carrying the air of a closing set on a German mountainside—a rave reshape of Caspar David Friedrich's quintessential painting  Wanderer above the Sea of Fog —wind sweeping around you until a hardgroove bassline introduces an element of steeliness, the summit re-cast in girders and concrete. 

There's also plenty of dubbier, womb-like moments to offset the twitchy mood. Take "Miiiiiii": the pads hold steady but never stop shifting, and beneath them sits what sounds like a springtime field recording, birds chirping into a soft kick drum. "Ziiiiiiiii" has a lighter touch still, like the lovechild of a SnPLO and Dettinger record left out to gather dust—the cycle home from a long night, the melody a hazy sun coming up, the percussion your own worn-out legs chugging you back. "Leeeeee" bridges the two worlds, and gets closer to traditional dub techno than anything else here:  Shinichi Atobe 's warmth over the pure dub glimmer of Vainqueur.

On the dub techno continuum, Picture sits closer to  Convextion  than to most of the '90s set, in both spirit and sound. Whereas Convextion once described his own music as "emotional punishment," on  Uuuuuuuu , I'd suggest Picture hits emotional levity. The material is heavy and the arrangements are crowded, yet the swing keeps everything off the floor: unquantised, the same weight stops pressing down and starts lifting. It's been on  our minds  lately that the 2020s might lack a sound of their own, that the decade has spent itself revisiting other people's halcyon days. Zaks' restless take on dub techno is proof there's still evolution inside the framework, and thrilling stuff still lies ahead.

items.body: Las Instancias comprises Shantala Ferreyra on clarinet, Fermín Suárez on double bass, and Gonzalo Goicoechea on drums. Ferreyra is an Argentinian clarinettist and composer who graduated from the Jazz Performance Program at the Manuel de Falla Conservatory in 2024. In 2025, she released her debut album featuring her original compositions performed by her quintet, and in 2026, she was awarded a scholarship to study composition in Basel, Switzerland. Her work combines composition and improvisation. Suárez is a double bass player, improviser, songwriter, and composer from Rosario, Argentina. His artistic work encompasses a wide range of genres, including jazz, tango, Argentine folk, improvised music, and classical, often mixing, stretching, and breaking the limits between languages and traditions. He co-created the punk-tango and avant-garde ensemble ‘La Rompiente’ for which he composes and arranges. In 2026, he started the solo project ‘Ola de sótano’, a double bass and vocals set with electronics, featuring songs, improvisations and spoken word. He’s also a frequent collaborator of composer and pianist Rocío Giménez López. Goicoechea is a drummer and educator specializing in jazz. He began his studies at the Leopoldo Marechal School of Arts and later continued at the Manuel de Falla Conservatory. Since 2021, he has performed with a variety of jazz-oriented ensembles. After a year devoted to live performance and composition, Las Instancias is released by the Argentine label 625 Discos, and captures the result of their ongoing collaboration so far. With no harmonic instrument, the trio leans into timbre, register, and the register distances between clarinet, bass, and drums. The pared-back format serves as the foundation upon which the group builds its identity and scribes its musical language. The ensemble work their way through various compositions (mostly written by Ferreyra and Suárez) that constantly flirt with the edges of jazz and improvised music, exploring their aesthetic possibilities and different orchestration combinations. Recorded during a session in Rosario, the album seeks to become a living reflection of a live performance, with all its nuances and dynamism. There are fierce solos rooted in jazz language contrasted with moments of introspection expressed through a more abstract idiom, all while maintaining a strong sense of tension and attention. There is a sense of a group whose members perform in proximity, without separation or post-production tricks. The recording is an intimate encounter between both the musicians and the listener. The absence of a harmonic instrument becomes a presence: a framework that pushes them toward inventive orchestration, elastic structures, and an exploration of musical language. This album contains some standout solos and ensemble work. There is a subliminal quality to this trio that makes the music fun, as well as profoundly interesting to listen to. Don’t be fooled by the opening bars of the first track. ‘Lampara Nueva’ starts like a traditional jazz piece, but develops into something extraordinary, the dialogue flowing between the clarinet, bass and percussion like water, flowing back and forth, with a swing here, a change there, and something just for the heck of it anywhere you might care to drop in. There is a taste of traditional jazz, particularly in the drum solos that emerge from the ensemble work, particularly in the second half of the number, but there is also much free playing. ‘Mucho Agora Mismo’ starts with a gentle bass solo and works itself into a frenzy, the clarinet delivering fiery solos across the percussion, with many variations in between. This is a track of many parts, blended seamlessly together. Just beautiful. ‘Dos Veces Agosto’ is a track of harmonies, rhythms, and counter-rhythms, with some bass solos, clarinet that works around the theme, and explores many musical avenues, while maintaining a connection with the central theme. ‘En Meyo’ is a clarinet solo track, with Ferreyra meditating on a theme, while ‘Ok/Off’ is a track where all three instruments lock into the same rhythmic pattern, creating a hypnotic dynamic. A bowed bass emerges, warm and resonant, before the trio returns to their lively, idea‑trading interplay. ‘Pegao’ is introduced by a bowed bass solo, over which the clarinet drops, adding light touches and a rapid change of texture, which the drums enhance, adding their own feel and colour. It is worth listening to this for the changes and rhythmic patterns that evolve, disappear, and re-emerge, led largely by the bass, whose voice is central to this number. The album closes with a second take of 'Mucho agora mismo' which is extravagant and allows each musician to deliver improvised music of the highest calibre. Las Instancias are three musicians whose shared curiosity has shaped a sound that feels both stripped back and richly alive. There’s a cohesion that makes the music both fun and deeply absorbing. You hear three musicians who trust each other enough to take risks — to push, to pull, to leave space, to fill it, to let the music breathe and then ignite. It’s intimate, inventive, and full of personality. Las instancias by Las instancias Get it on vinyl here: https://elasticstage.com/625discos/releases/las-instancias-album Email This BlogThis! items.body: Label: Temperphantom, 2026 Personnel - Victor Vieira-Branco: vibraphone; Sam Yulsman: piano; John Moran: double bass; Joey Sullivan: drums. Playing the vibraphone with a relentless sense of urgency and intent while displaying a strong, distinctive compositional identity, Victor Vieira-Branco is a name to reckon with in contemporary jazz. Rooted in Philadelphia, Bark Culture is Vieira-Branco’s creative brainchild, where intriguing sonic forces feel at once dark and lyrical, sometimes effusive yet always fresh and compelling. For this date, the core trio—with John Moran on double bass and Joey Sullivan on drums—is expanded into a harmonically richer quartet with the addition of pianist Sam Yulsman. The Giant is Awkward , Bark Culture’s sophomore record, opens with “ Palace ”, whose lush theme, rhythmically vivid drive, and hip arrangement command our attention from the very first minute. The bandleader’s rolling liquidity blends seamlessly with sweeping keyboard gestures and the vibrant tangle woven by bass and drums. Sullivan does an intricate, actively propulsive job throughout, fueled by alternative-rock stamina and responsive fills. Yulsman’s “ Farce ”, the only piece not written by Vieira-Branco, is kinetic, asymmetric, and daring in its construction, pervaded by a thrilling sense of uncertainty and a fair dose of arcane postmodern psychedelia. “ Willow ” holds a powerful and consistently engaging backbone that is unafraid of odd meters and metric modulation. Impeccably framed by Yulsman’s off-kilter piano (which sounds great despite being slightly out of tune) and Vieira-Branco’s hallucinogenic vibraphone, the piece climaxes into an unpredictable, stratospheric concentration of sound. On a different register, “ Panic ” gives silence an important role, developing with a balladic feel that favors spacious atmospheres. The album closes with “ Spectrum ”, where the beauty of the instrumentation creates ebbs and flows through intricate accentuation that feels simultaneously startling and exhilarating. There’s space for drum talk before the tension mounts through authoritative bowed bass, nebulous vibraphone streams, dreamy piano sequences, and jittery drumming. With each member focused on injecting energy and emotion, Bark Culture pushes the envelope, reinventing itself as an experimental group that strikes a perfect balance between written material and open improvisation. Vieira-Branco steps forward impressively on The Giant Is Awkward , and it’s remarkable to think these pieces were recorded at the last minute while still in sketch form. items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

According to its founder, Eugene Rodriguez, who also sings and plays on the record, Los Cenzontles is a �musical group and non-profit organization, which I founded over thirty years ago.�  As he continues in the album�s liner notes, the group �has a long history of producing projects exploring Mexico�s deep roots and our connections with various traditions that, so far, have included Irish, Louisiana Creole, Cuban, American cowboy, classical, pop, rock, and blues�, the latest of which is
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
. Los Cenzontles translates to the mockingbird, or, from its Aztec root word, the bird of four hundred voices. This is a fitting name for the range of musical diversity represented here.
With songs sung in Spanish, Hawaiian, and English, the concept traces back to the legacy of Mexican cowboys who travelled from California to the Hawaiian Islands to wrangle the long-horned cattle introduced there in the nineteenth century. They also brought the guitar. The 16 tracks feature old Hawaiian songs with new Spanish lyrics, old Mexican songs with new Hawaiian lyrics, new compositions, and traditional Americana. Yet it is an entirely cohesive musical package held together by dense arrangements of ukuleles, guitars, Mexican harp, and accordion.
Sonny Lim & David Hidalgo
Besides their distinctive voices, the headline artists Taj Mahal and David Hidalgo provide the gravitas and musicianship that their long and distinguished careers have earned. According to the liner notes, they were the catalysts behind the project and facilitated the choice of songs, arrangements, and played a range of instruments. On vocals they are joined by Hawaiian natives Gary Haleamau, Sheldeen Haleamau, Sonny Lim, and long-time Cenzontles member Fabiola Trujillo.
Deportee
To give a taste of the sessions, included before the traditional �Fishin� Blues� is Taj Mahal teaching the musicians how to play it. Sung by David Hildalgo,  the lovely �A Matter of Time� comes from the 1984 album
Will the Wolf Survive
by his most famous project, Los Lobos. Another standout for me, �Navegar� features a slack string guitar solo reminiscent of Duane Eddie and one of many tasty lap steel turns by Sonny Lim. Their interpretation of Woody Guthrie's �Deportee� moves into social commentary, highlighting the cruel realities of being a migrant worker in America.
Vaquero Paniolo
Recorded over five days, mostly live in one room at the Los Cenzontles headquarters in San Pablo, California, including the talents of some of their academy�s students, the recording has real spontaneity to it. Arrangements are stretched by improvisations, sometimes by several different instruments on a single tune. The project also represents a great spirit of cooperation and diversity of language, culture, age, and gender. It includes the inputs of musical legends, seasoned pros, and amateurs. The wonderfully rich and often stereotyped musical cultures of both Mexico and Hawaii are represented here with the authenticity of lived experience.
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
is a worthy addition to Los Cenzontles� important work. Quoting Rodriguez again, �Culture is a fabric within which we are all woven.�

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Weird and wonderful, it sounds like they rooted through an attic full of 78 RPM records, scribbled down some arrangements, and then played them on a collection of instruments they found in another attic, including accordion, sax, xylophone, clarinet, banjo, ukulele, theremin, Hawaiian guitar, bagpipe chanter (I�m guessing here), and musical saw.

The 27 short tracks are mostly voiced by Cravic, who talk-sings in the manner of an everyman Maurice Chevalier. He is often accompanied by the accordion, a customary instrument in the bal-musette style that remains a strong element of the eclectic range of styles they have managed to synthesize. They also include ragtime, jug, French chanson, and, to my ears, skiffle,  just to get the list started.

The liner notes point out that �Les Crimes du Musette is also a gold mine for scholars, a veritable treasure trove.� Exploring the treasures is beyond my scope here, as each tune has a long history. A highlight for me is the humorous �Ukulele Lady� from 1925, which first delighted me on Arlo Guthrie�s 1971 album

Tiny Sun creates tiny songs that give off light and heat well out of proportion to their size. Composed, performed, and produced by Martina Sorbara, Jonathan Goldsmith, and Don Rooke, the record is vaguely Americana, with plucked guitars and ukuleles, chiming keyboards, and the lonesome slide of the guitar.
Vanishment
contains eighteen sparkling miniatures - that take a scant 34 minutes to negotiate - notable for their economy of arrangement and the subtle directness of the lyrics. The tracks glow with Martina�s clear, high, and sometimes fragile voice.
The songs are about loss: lost love, lost confidence, but sometimes about resignation to the enigmatic quirks of the world. The tone of wry fatalism mirrors the fact that this project is the work of many years of collaboration and email exchanges while the trio pursued their musical day jobs. Jonathan Goldsmith is an award-winning composer for television and film, Don Rooke fronts the Toronto roots band The Henrys, and Martina Sorbara is known for folk, electropop, and her band Dragonette.
Kerosene Madrigal
The range of backgrounds leads to many styles, and the record betrays interesting influences. The opening track, �Kerosene Madrigal,� is a sort of miner�s blues reminiscent of Michelle Shocked. The soul-country of �Imagined Love� reminded me of fellow Torontonians Cowboy Junkies, especially the sweet organ. The stoic and twangy �Don�t Fault the Stars for Falling� could have been a Dolly Parton tune.
A Grand Expanse
�A Grand Expanse� has a more ambitious arrangement.  It sounds like the end-credits song from a long-ago film we only vaguely remember. It says everything it needs to in one minute and twenty seconds and exactly 38 words. It is quintessential Tiny Sun.
The entire recording feels like music from a dream, and since no one knows exactly what dream music sounds like, this could be it.

items.body: In August 1819, tens of thousands of working men and women gathered in St. Peter�s Field in Manchester to hear the politician Henry Hunt speak. They were difficult times, many still out of work after the Napoleonic wars, rising prices and low wages � and always those at the bottom of the heap suffering. Hunt was a famed orator, a man on the side of the people, able to stir and inspire with his voice. Although the gathering was peaceful, the size of the crowd terrified the magistrates, who panicked and imagined an uprising. They sent in half-trained dragoons and the cavalry, who rode down, slashed and killed without compunction or compassion. In the end, 18 died and up to 700 were wounded. It was a stain on the nation, an outrage; prompting Percy Shelley, one of the poetic giants of the age, to write The Masque of Anarchy , with its famous lines: �Rise like Lions after slumber / in unvanquishable number / She your chains to earth like dew / Which in sleep had fallen on you / Ye are many - they are few.� Peterloo, as people called it, remains one of the seminal events in English working-class history, one that Sean Cooney of the Young 'Uns has revisited for this album of original songs, which is lavishly presented in a book with contemporary letters, political cartoons and illustrations to create a multimedia event. It�s ambitious, no doubt about that, and he�s selected some great talent to help � guitarist Sam Carter, the almost ubiquitous fiddler/singer Eliza Carthy, Ben Nicholls supplying background and texture on various instruments, and the Lancashire industrial ballad singer Jennifer Reid, who doubles as narrator. Peter's Field by Sean Cooney, Eliza Carthy, Sam Carter, Jennifer Reid For a small ensemble, they make a powerful noise. The songs capture the feel of the day; the anticipation and excitement at the summer gathering, the joy that turns to terror and flight as the troops charge, then the bitter, mournful aftermath, voiced some powerful melodies and very well-chosen images. As a writer, Cooney often focuses on the personal in the small tales of people like �Sam Bamford� and �Mary Fildes,� while the three short pieces that comprise �The Monkey Rides The Mare� capture the bluster and arrogance of the soldiers. Peter's Field by Sean Cooney, Eliza Carthy, Sam Carter, Jennifer Reid Cooney is a persuasive singer, and on this heartfelt project, he puts plenty of emotion into his voice. Having two other outstanding vocalists alongside him makes for a wonderful triple threat. In these days when governments across the world are cracking down on protest, this stands as a sobering and very timely reminder. It�s a history lesson, yes, but the detail of the history stays in the book, while the music creates a set of songs that will resonate and remain for a long time. Find the artist online. items.body:
Live at Rockpalast 1999
documents a command performance at the Loreley open-air amphitheater by Malcolm �Mac� Rebennack Jr., aka Dr. John. Rockpalast is a live-music TV show broadcast since 1974 by Westdeutscher Rundfunk (WDR), the archival source for this CD-DVD package, and coincidentally a remarkable cultural institution on its own terms.
Taped at the height of Dr. John�s international popularity, backing the singer-pianist-guitarist are New Orleans stalwarts Bobby Broom (guitar), David Barard (bass), and Herman Ernest (drums), a tight quartet that projects authority and engages the crowd from start to close.
A striking UNESCO-designated World Heritage Site set, the Loreley is a slate pinnacle on a mythic horseshoe bend of the Rhine River, memorializing an enduring German literary legend both tragic and romantic. The setting is thus well-suited for Mac�s mystical spirit and lyrical style. By this stage of his career, he characterized his live show as a Mardi Gras revue with a mix of New Orleans standards and some of his most recognizable compositions.
Hence, he opens with the NOLA classic �Iko, Iko,� a half-sung, half-chanted celebration of community participation in the renowned Mardi Gras second-line street procession. Then comes the in-your-face boast �Qualified,� wherein the singer warns, �I got the power to control / I can see clean through you, blind mole / I want to tell you now, I'm qualified / You know that I'm qualified.�
Any Dr. John fan will recognize �I Walk on Guilded Splinters,� a moody, percussively insistent, foreboding expression of the Night Tripper�s immersion in �funknology� (his term), gris-gris herbology, and hoodoo incantation, punctuated with jungle growls and cries, a loopy, spooky slide whistle, and an extended psych-guitar solo: �Walk thru the fire / Fly thru the smoke / See my enemy / At the end of dey rope.�
Every piece in this well- honed set deserves considertion. Although Dr John lived for many years in Los Angeles and New York, his enduring hometown connection shows in the fond inclusion of his own �Sweet Home New Orleans� and �Goin� Back to New Orleans,� and he nods to a key influence with a funky rendering of Duke Ellington�s �I'm Gonna Go Fishin�.� Among other gems are Mac�s Top�10 hit �Right Place, Wrong Time,� and the instantly recognizable closer, Earl King�s �Big Chief,� another Mardi Gras burner.
Regarding his live performance approach, per the notes, �I always play a little bit of everything. I think that�s what music�s about: a little bit of somethin� old, somethin� in the middle, somethin� new, and somethin� as yet uncreated.�
Dr John's�s longtime fans will welcome this archival gem, which also is a solid introduction for any late comers to the party. Surmounting the barriers of language and culture, the power of
At the Rockpalast
is also evident in the enthusiastic audience response. As he declares, �If you�re gonna get off on somethin� you don�t need to know nothin� about it. Music is a universal language.�

Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items.body: Editor's note: When this set of recordings came to me, I was at a loss as to how to share it. It's not music, in any traditional sense (although there is some freestyle rapping), and a 'review' of such an artifact of reality seems superfluous to the content. Instead, I asked sound recordist Ian Brennan if I could simply use his own brief commentary and the recordings he made on the street in Chicago. Twenty-five people afflicted by gun violence participated, many from the very block we�d setup on. Many neighbors were pulled-in spontaneously. Almost every one in the community had been impacted by violence somehow� both on the receiving and the inflicting end, and many both. One woman had just come from a memorial service, another was on her way. That�s how far-reaching the violence. Almost no one went untouched. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors By chance, we convened on the day that Trump ordered the deployment of the National Guard to the city. The recording took place on the front porch of the leader's ninety-four-year-old grandmother's house�right in the heart of the ��hood,� beneath the Midway Airport�s landing path. A pair of stray pitfalls stalked the block. But the grandmother warned not of gunshots, but the mosquitoes in her yard. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors We were in a section of town that one man defined as �the forgotten parts.� Just a short jaunt from the designer clothes shops and posh hotels of the city�s Magnificent Mile, the Southside spawned such legendary Blues artists as Muddy Waters, Willie Dixon, and Howlin� Wolf. Jazz musicians like Lionel Hampton and even Benny Goodman, hailed from nearby. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors The participants ranged in age from seventeen to sixty-seven, but the pattern held true. The person who�d asserted �you�ll really want to hear my story,� was the least compelling. The reluctant, the most moving. One elder�s tough facade broke down as she shared how she�d lost both her sons. She tearfully apologized, �I�m sorry. I�m sorry. I�m sorry.� But she had nothing to be sorry for. Society is the one that owes the apology� for the staggering statistical inequities of which no reasonable defense can be made. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors Editor's note: The full set of recordings are available on Bandcamp. Any profits from this project will be donated to Cure Violence Global , who states that their mission is "advancing an evidence-based health approach to end violence globally." When I asked him about the background sounds, producer Ian Brennan added, "No music is added. It�s all sounds from the source environment. I also ran loops/drones on a different track in the background as they spoke, and when they ended up being incidentally/somewhat magically/eerily synchronous, that is what was used for a few pieces with 'accompaniment' like some of the rap freestyles."
